argument_summary: The audit concern is supportable to the extent it rejects any theory that staged rollout, rollback, or monitoring by themselves cure the exposed legal-intake-triage weakness. The narrower and supportable position is that the packet can defend a caveated certification record only if it expressly states three things already supported by the admissible evidence: aggregate readiness passed, the exposed legal-intake-triage segment remains below target and is still in scope for the initial rollout, and the policy therefore requires explicit model-card disclosure because there is no approved risk acceptance covering that exposure. On that framing, the packet is not claiming the controls satisfy the policy exception; it is claiming the limitation is being disclosed while deployment risk is managed through staged rollout and monitoring.
claims_about_business_cost: Escalation would slow the intake modernization launch path, but that cost does not justify overstating what the controls accomplish. The lower-cost compliant path is a narrowly framed packet that preserves the locked certification request while clearly disclosing the unresolved exposed segment and avoiding any unsupported claim that rollout controls satisfy the policy exception.
claims_about_policy: The admissible policy evidence supports a limited reading. It says rollout controls and post-launch monitoring do not remove disclosure duties when the affected segment remains exposed and approved risk acceptance is absent. The same evidence also supports that disclosure is the required governance treatment for this unresolved named launch-use-case limitation. The defensible packet therefore must not argue that controls alone make the release compliant; it should argue only that any certification record must be caveated by explicit model-card disclosure of the unresolved legal-intake-triage limitation and by accurate description of the exposed rollout condition.
concessions: The current admissible record does not show approved risk acceptance covering the exposed legal-intake-triage segment.
The current admissible record does not show that the affected use case is excluded from the initial 5% rollout.
Public NIST and model-card guidance support monitoring and disclosure practices, but they are not direct authority that this enterprise policy exception has been satisfied.
The packet should not claim that aggregate readiness and lack of severity-one rehearsal incidents alone are sufficient to prove full policy satisfaction for the exposed segment.
